strengths: Slide 1 establishes a memorable, brief-specific premise with the fixed/linked/variable sequence, a strong thesis, and a clearly labeled conceptual image rather than presenting it as archival evidence.
Slides 3–4 use relevant historical artifacts, visible source links, and careful captions that distinguish reproduction or modern-browser rendering from period evidence.

Slides 5–7 move beyond prose through a color-coded comparison table, a computational workflow, and a persistence diagram; slide 7 particularly supports the argument that media accumulate rather than simply replace one another.
Slide 8 converts the lecture into a credible studio exercise for design students, while the dark opening and closing slides create purposeful bookends.

issues.evidence: The four surrounding blocks identify components of a medium, but their speech-bubble-like tails and equal placement do not reveal how tools, infrastructure, interfaces, and conventions act on one another; much of the diagram repeats the adjacent prose.
issues.fix: Add directional relationships or a concrete worked example showing how a change in one component pressures the other three.

issues.evidence: The screenshot itself is legible only as a page-level artifact at presentation size, while the pale gray caption is small and low-contrast for projection.
issues.fix: Enlarge or crop one linked region for analysis and increase caption contrast and size.

issues.evidence: The six chevrons visually describe a linear pipeline, although the text says that evaluation updates the next constraints. The return loop exists only in prose, and no actual output variants demonstrate what changes.
issues.fix: Draw the feedback path from human judgment and revision back to constraints, and show two or three visibly different outputs from the same conditions.

issues.evidence: The horizontal bars begin at different positions and can initially read as an undocumented chronology even though the footer calls them schematic overlap.
issues.fix: Use nested layers or explicit continuity markers so accumulation is apparent without relying on the caveat.

A.signatureMoment: Slide 7 combines three era-specific trade-off cards with an accumulation diagram, making the deck’s central “persistence, not replacement” argument visible rather than merely stated.

strengths: Slide 1 is a disciplined editorial opening: the oversized headline, restrained orange accent, and three-state line establish the lecture structure without clutter.
Slides 3–4 present the print and early-Web artifacts with visible attribution and explicit caveats about reproduction and modern-browser rendering.
Slide 5 is an efficient reference table with strong alignment and restrained hierarchy, suitable for note-taking in a university lecture.
Slide 8 gives design students a usable critique framework and studio brief rather than ending with a generic summary.

issues.evidence: The evenly spaced three-node line resembles a chronological timeline but provides no dates or indication that the spacing is conceptual; this sits uneasily with the later claim that the eras overlap.
issues.fix: Label it explicitly as a conceptual progression or encode overlap rather than equal temporal spacing.

issues.evidence: The donut and icons name four components but do not show reciprocal pressure between them, despite the text’s central claim that changing one affects the others. The example note is also small for projection.
issues.fix: Replace the static donut with a relational diagram and integrate the browser example into the diagram at readable size.

issues.evidence: The large uncropped browser screenshot contains text too small to inspect from a lecture audience, while the explanatory caption is pale and small.
issues.fix: Pair the full-page view with a magnified callout showing hyperlinks and possible reading routes.

issues.evidence: The key promise of “many outputs” is represented only by three gray text rows—“Condensed,” “Expanded,” and “Reframed.” Human judgment and revision sit in a separate strip with no visible feedback arrow, and the blue emoji-like revision glyph is inconsistent with the otherwise restrained icon system.
issues.fix: Show actual contrasting visual outputs and connect revision back to conditions with a clear loop; replace the emoji glyph with a typographic or drawn symbol.

issues.evidence: The slide announces “A contemporary artifact” and “One poster contains all three,” but no poster is shown. The generic concentric circles therefore carry an argument that the promised evidence never demonstrates.
issues.fix: Replace the circles with an annotated real poster or interface, marking its inherited print hierarchy, networked distribution, and computational variation.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 6 has the deck’s strongest explanatory composition—a conditions-to-model-to-variations sequence—but it stops short of showing the variations or the feedback loop it describes.

result.reason: Both decks pass the hard checks: each covers print, digital, and computational media in a restrained lecture format; neither shows clipping, missing assets, harmful distortion, or unflagged fabricated evidence. Viewed independently and in either order, A remains preferable because its opening thesis, comparative structures, accumulation argument, and closing exercise form a more memorable teaching arc. B is clean and competent but repeatedly substitutes labels for evidence, most notably the unseen “contemporary artifact” on slide 7. The single most valuable improvement to B would be replacing that generic diagram with an annotated real artifact that visibly combines all three media logics. Route identity is withheld, so the original arm cannot be identified; the additional visible complexity in A is mostly earned through clearer pacing and more useful variation. A exceeds competent default quality modestly, but its abstract computational section prevents sustained wow.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: Build the middle around one rigorously annotated case study transformed across all three eras: show the same message as a fixed print composition, a linked interactive interface, and several outputs from a computational system. Overlay the grids, reading paths, production roles, and feedback loops so the historical transformation becomes directly inspectable rather than mostly schematic.
